label: Lost the fight
title: Defeated Generals
dek: Six generals who reached the deciding battle of their war and lost it, ranked from the most embarrassing defeat to the most impressive.
summary: A ranking of six generals who lost the deciding battle of their war, from Cornwallis at Yorktown to Hannibal at Zama.

blocks.text: 6. Charles Cornwallis
Yorktown, Virginia · 1781 · NO-SHOW

Britain’s top general in the American Revolution got trapped at Yorktown by George Washington and the French navy. His surrender all but ended the war. He skipped the ceremony, said he was sick and sent his deputy instead. Then he spent years blaming his boss in print. Britain gave him India to run anyway. Failed upward, in writing.
War: American Revolution · America won
5. Publius Quinctilius Varus
Teutoburg, Germany · 9 CE · WARNED

Rome sent Varus to tame Germany. His trusted local adviser, Arminius, was secretly planning an ambush. Varus was warned and didn’t listen. Arminius led three Roman legions into a forest trap, and almost no one came out. Rome never conquered Germany. The historian Suetonius says Emperor Augustus banged his head on a door yelling, “Varus, give me back my legions!”
War: Rome vs. German tribes · Germans won
4. Marcus Licinius Crassus
Carrhae, Turkey · 53 BCE · PAY-TO-WIN

The richest man in Rome, and a partner of Julius Caesar. Money wasn’t enough. He wanted Caesar-level glory, so he started a war with the Parthian Empire to the east. Their horseback archers wiped out his army, and he was killed. A historian writing almost 300 years later says they poured molten gold into his mouth. We’re filing that as “alleged.”
War: Rome vs. Parthia · Parthia won
3. Harold Godwinson
Hastings, England · 1066 · NO REST

In 1066, England got invaded twice in one month. King Harold beat a Norwegian army in the north, one that included his own rebel brother. Then he raced about 250 miles south to fight William of Normandy at Hastings. Harold lost and died. William became “the Conqueror,” and French words flooded into English. Some of that was bad luck. Some of it was Harold.
War: Norman Conquest · William took England
2. Napoleon Bonaparte
Waterloo, Belgium · 1815 · COMEBACK

Napoleon crowned himself emperor of France and conquered much of Europe. Beaten in 1814, he was exiled to Elba, a small island off Italy. He escaped, took back France and lasted about 100 days before losing at Waterloo to the British and Prussians. Island No. 2, St. Helena, sat about 1,200 miles off Africa. He never left.
War: Napoleonic Wars · Napoleon out for good
1. Hannibal Barca
Zama, now Tunisia · 202 BCE · GOAT

rows: Told his city to make peace

blocks.text: Hannibal led the army of Carthage, a North African city that was Rome’s great rival. He marched an army, elephants included, over the Alps into Italy. At Cannae he wiped out a much bigger Roman army in one day, one of the worst days in Rome’s history. For about 15 years Rome couldn’t beat him in Italy. It finally did back in Africa, at Zama. Hannibal then told Carthage to take the peace deal, the most gracious thing anyone in this book does. Armies still study Cannae today.
War: The Second Punic War · Rome became the Mediterranean’s top power
Skill counts in their favor. Excuses count against them. Blaming someone else in writing counts double.
No. 6 is the loss with the least to admire. No. 1 is the loser people still study.

sources: Rome, Varus and Crassus. Tacitus, Annals; Suetonius, Life of Augustus; Cassius Dio, Roman History; Livy, History of Rome, Books 21–22 (Hannibal).

Augustus’s “Varus, give me back my legions!” is Suetonius. The molten gold poured into Crassus’s mouth comes from a historian writing almost 300 years later (Cassius Dio), and we label it “alleged.” Harold, Napoleon and Cornwallis draw on the sources listed under Letters to the AI Dead, Not a Loser. Not Short. Not Alone., and Two Generals, One Printing Press.
